narrative:
Your application was denied because the model estimated a 56% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt—slightly more likely than not. Under the admission rule used, that prediction was enough to reject your application.

The strongest concern was your part-time status. Among admitted students, nearly all—92.8%—were full-time, while only 7.2% were part-time, and this factor pushed your prediction most strongly toward failure. The next most influential factor was your undergraduate GPA of 2.40, well below the admitted-student average of 3.23, which also pushed toward failure. Your upper-middle family income worked in the opposite direction, toward passing; it is common among admitted students, but its influence was weaker than the other two and could not offset them.

To improve a future application, strengthen your academic record through additional rigorous coursework or a graduate credential, prepare carefully to raise your LSAT score, and show a realistic full-time study plan with strong academic support. Meet with admissions advising to discuss what evidence would demonstrate readiness, and consider retaking the exam or applying after a sustained record of improved performance.
